subject: chemistry
title: Metallic bonding
summary: The electron-sea model of metallic bonding and how it explains the properties of metals, the reactivity series, how alloys and heat treatment change metals, and the limitations of the model including for nanomaterials.
body:
Metals are everywhere in daily life: copper in electrical wiring, aluminium in drink cans, steel in bridges and gold in jewellery. They share a set of properties, such as conducting electricity, bending without breaking and shining, and all of these come from the same simple idea about how metal atoms are bonded together. This lesson explains that model, uses it to explain metal properties, and shows how chemists change metals to suit particular uses.

## Think of it like this

### Metallic bonding is like a share house pooling its money

Imagine a share house where every housemate puts their spare cash into one shared kitty that anyone can use. Each metal atom does something similar: it puts its **valence electrons** into a shared "sea" that belongs to the whole lump of metal, leaving the atom as a positive **cation**. The shared kitty is what keeps the household together, just as the attraction between the cations and the **delocalised electrons** is the **metallic bond**. And because the money can move freely around the whole house, it's like how the electrons can flow through the metal and carry an electric current.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* electrons aren't spent or used up, and the "glue" isn't sharing but **electrostatic attraction** between positive cations and negative electrons. Also, the electrons only drift in one direction when a voltage is applied; otherwise they move about randomly.

### Bending a metal is like pushing marbles through honey

Picture a tray of marbles packed in rows and covered in honey. Push the top row sideways and the marbles roll into new positions, but the honey still surrounds every one of them, so the tray doesn't fall apart. In a metal, the layers of cations slide past each other when a force is applied, and the electron sea moves with them, keeping the attraction in every direction. That's why metals are **malleable** and **ductile** instead of shattering like an ionic crystal.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* honey holds marbles because it's thick and sticky, while the electron sea holds cations by electrostatic attraction. Real metals also contain **grains** and defects, so how easily they bend depends on their grain structure, not just on sliding layers.

### Alloys are like a car park with utes and motorbikes added

Picture a car park full of identical cars lined up neatly, so a whole row can be shuffled along easily. In a **substitutional alloy** like brass, some cars are swapped for utes of a similar but different size: the rows are now uneven. In an **interstitial alloy** like steel, small motorbikes (carbon atoms) are squeezed into the gaps between cars (iron cations). Either way, the rows can't slide past each other as smoothly, so the alloy is **harder and stronger** but less malleable than the pure metal.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* atoms aren't parked in marked bays; they form a 3D lattice held by metallic bonding. Alloying can also change other properties, such as resistance to corrosion in stainless steel, which a car park picture doesn't explain.

### In real life

The copper wiring in the walls of your house relies on delocalised electrons to carry current, and aluminium foil shows how malleable a metal can be when it's rolled very thin. Stainless steel cutlery and kitchen sinks resist rusting because the chromium in the alloy forms a protective oxide layer.

## Key ideas

### The electron-sea model

Metal atoms have few valence electrons (usually 1, 2 or 3) and low ionisation energies, so they lose these electrons easily. In a solid metal, each atom releases its valence electrons, which no longer belong to any single atom. The result is described by the **electron-sea model**:

- a three-dimensional **lattice** (a regular repeating arrangement) of **cations** (positive metal ions),
- surrounded by a "sea" of **delocalised electrons**, which are free to move throughout the whole structure.

**Metallic bonding** is the electrostatic attraction between the positive metal cations and the delocalised electrons around them. It is non-directional: each cation is attracted to the electron sea in all directions, not to one particular neighbour. The cations are packed closely together in the lattice.

### Explaining the properties of metals

| Property | Explanation using the model |
|---|---|
| **Electrical conductivity** (in solid and liquid states) | Delocalised electrons are charged and free to move. When a voltage is applied, they drift towards the positive terminal, carrying current. |
| **Thermal conductivity** | The free-moving electrons, and the closely packed vibrating cations, transfer kinetic energy rapidly through the metal. |
| **Malleability** (can be hammered into sheets) and **ductility** (can be drawn into wires) | When a force is applied, layers of cations slide past each other. Because the electron sea moves with them and the bonding is non-directional, the attraction is maintained and the metal changes shape instead of breaking. |
| **Lustre** (shiny surface) | Delocalised electrons absorb and re-emit light at the surface, so freshly cut metal reflects light. |
| **High melting and boiling points** (for most metals) | Strong electrostatic attraction between cations and delocalised electrons extends throughout the lattice, so a lot of energy is needed to separate the particles. |
| **High density** (for most metals) | Cations are closely packed. |

Melting points vary widely. Mercury is liquid at room temperature and the group 1 metals melt at low temperatures, while tungsten melts above 3400 °C. In general, metallic bonding is stronger when cations have a higher charge (more delocalised electrons per cation) and are smaller. This is why magnesium (Mg²⁺) has a higher melting point than sodium (Na⁺), and why melting points of group 1 metals decrease down the group as the cations get larger.

### Reactivity of metals

Metals react by **losing** electrons to form positive ions. A metal is more reactive if it loses its valence electrons more easily, which links to low ionisation energy, low core charge and large atomic radius. This explains why group 1 metals are more reactive than group 2 metals in the same period, and why reactivity increases down groups 1 and 2.

A **reactivity series** lists metals in order of how readily they react. A common version (most to least reactive) is:

`K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Sn > Pb > Cu > Ag > Au`

The series can be built from experiments:

- **Reaction with water**: potassium and sodium react vigorously with cold water; calcium reacts steadily; magnesium reacts only slowly with cold water but faster with steam.

`2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g)`

- **Reaction with dilute acid**: metals above hydrogen in the series (such as Mg, Zn and Fe) produce hydrogen gas; copper, silver and gold do not react with dilute hydrochloric acid.

`Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)`

- **Reaction with oxygen**: reactive metals tarnish quickly in air, while gold stays shiny for centuries.

`2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s)`

- **Displacement reactions**: a more reactive metal will displace a less reactive metal from a solution of its ions.

`Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s)`

In this reaction, zinc loses electrons and copper(II) ions gain them, so a reddish-brown copper coating forms on the zinc and the blue colour of the solution fades. Copper placed in zinc sulfate solution shows no reaction.

Aluminium appears less reactive than its position suggests because a thin, tough layer of aluminium oxide forms on its surface and protects it.

### Modifying metals

Pure metals are often too soft for practical use, because their uniform layers of cations slide easily. Chemists change their properties in two main ways.

**Alloys**. An **alloy** is a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements (metals or non-metals).

- In a **substitutional alloy**, atoms of a similar size replace some of the metal atoms in the lattice. Example: brass (copper and zinc), bronze (copper and tin).
- In an **interstitial alloy**, much smaller atoms fit into the gaps between metal cations. Example: steel, in which small carbon atoms sit between iron cations.

In both types, the different-sized particles disrupt the regular layers, so the layers can no longer slide past each other as easily. The alloy is harder and stronger but less malleable than the pure metal. Alloys can also resist corrosion better: stainless steel contains chromium, which forms a protective oxide layer.

**Work hardening and heat treatment**. Metals contain small regions called **crystals** or **grains**, each with a regular lattice. Treating a metal with heat changes the grain structure:

- **Annealing**: heating and then cooling slowly gives large crystals; the metal becomes softer and more ductile.
- **Quenching**: heating and then cooling rapidly (for example in cold water) gives small crystals; the metal becomes harder but more brittle.
- **Tempering**: gently reheating a quenched metal and cooling it reduces brittleness while keeping much of the hardness.
- **Work hardening**: repeatedly bending or hammering a metal at room temperature disrupts the grains, making it harder but also more brittle.

### Limitations of the model and nanomaterials

The electron-sea model is useful, but it is a simplification. It does not explain:

- why metals differ so greatly in melting point, hardness and conductivity,
- why some metals, such as iron, nickel and cobalt, are magnetic while others are not,
- why metals have different colours (for example gold and copper are not silvery).

**Nanomaterials** have structures between about 1 and 100 nanometres (1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m) in at least one dimension. **Metallic nanoparticles** have a very high surface area to volume ratio, so a large fraction of their atoms are at the surface. As a result, their properties can be quite different from those of the bulk metal. For example, gold nanoparticles can appear red or purple in solution rather than gold-coloured, and they can act as catalysts even though bulk gold is very unreactive. The simple electron-sea model, which assumes an extended lattice, cannot predict these size-dependent properties.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: explaining a property

Explain why copper is used for electrical wiring.

1. Identify the properties needed: conductivity and ductility (it must be drawn into wire).
2. Conductivity: copper's lattice contains delocalised electrons that are free to move and carry charge when a voltage is applied.
3. Ductility: when copper is drawn into a wire, layers of Cu²⁺ ions slide over each other; the delocalised electrons move with them, so the non-directional metallic bonding is maintained and the wire does not snap.

### Example 2: interpreting displacement results

A student places strips of metals X, Y and Z into solutions of each other's nitrates. X displaces both Y and Z. Y displaces Z but not X. Z displaces neither. Rank the metals.

1. A metal displaces another only if it is more reactive.
2. X displaces Y and Z, so X is more reactive than both.
3. Y displaces Z, so Y is more reactive than Z.
4. Order from most to least reactive: **X > Y > Z**.

### Example 3: comparing melting points

Explain why aluminium (melting point 660 °C) has a higher melting point than sodium (98 °C).

1. Aluminium forms Al³⁺ ions and contributes 3 delocalised electrons per atom; sodium forms Na⁺ and contributes 1.
2. Al³⁺ is also smaller than Na⁺.
3. A higher charge and smaller size give a stronger electrostatic attraction between the cations and the electron sea.
4. More energy is needed to disrupt this bonding, so aluminium melts at a higher temperature.

## Common mistakes

- Saying the lattice is made of neutral metal atoms. It is made of positive cations in a sea of delocalised electrons.
- Explaining conductivity with moving ions. In solid metals it is the delocalised electrons that move; the cations stay in place.
- Saying layers slide in a metal because the bonds break. The key point is that the bonding is non-directional and is maintained as the layers move.
- Assuming alloys are softer. Adding different-sized atoms makes sliding harder, so alloys are usually harder and stronger.
- Saying aluminium is unreactive. It is quite reactive but is protected by its oxide layer.

## Exam tips

- When explaining a property, always link a feature of the structure (delocalised electrons, closely packed cations, non-directional bonding) to the property. A property named without a structural reason earns little credit.
- Practise drawing a labelled electron-sea diagram: cations in a regular arrangement with electrons drawn between them and a key.
- Displacement data questions are common; remember that "no reaction" also gives information.
- Be prepared to compare heat treatments and to state the trade-off between hardness and brittleness.

## Tips to remember

- **"Positive ions in a sea of electrons"**: picture ping-pong balls (cations) floating in a pool of water (the delocalised electrons). The water holds them all together, in every direction.
- **Why metals bend but salt shatters**: in a metal, the layers slide and the electron "sea" flows with them, so the bonding is kept. In an ionic solid, sliding lines up like charges and it cracks.
- **Reactivity series K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Sn > Pb > Cu > Ag > Au** — a made-up memory trick: "**K**ind **N**ancy **Ca**n **M**ake **A** **Z**ebra **Fe**el **S**ad; **P**oor **Cu**te **S**ilver **G**oldfish" (Sn = tin, Pb = lead, Ag = silver, Au = gold).
- **"The bully takes the ions"**: in displacement, the more reactive metal pushes the less reactive one out of solution (Zn + CuSO₄ gives copper coating on the zinc; copper in ZnSO₄ does nothing).
- **Alloys are "speed bumps"**: different-sized atoms (brass: Cu + Zn substitutional; steel: small C atoms interstitial) stop the layers sliding, so alloys are harder and stronger.
- **Heat treatment rhyme — "Slow and soft, quick and brittle"**: annealing (cool slowly) → large crystals, softer; quenching (cool fast) → small crystals, harder but brittle; tempering eases the brittleness. (A made-up memory trick.)

## Key terms

- **Metallic bonding** — the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of metal cations and a sea of delocalised electrons.
- **Delocalised electrons** — valence electrons that are not attached to any one atom and are free to move throughout the structure.
- **Lattice** — a regular, repeating three-dimensional arrangement of particles.
- **Malleable** — able to be hammered or pressed into shape without breaking.
- **Ductile** — able to be drawn into a wire.
- **Lustre** — the shiny appearance of a freshly cut metal surface.
- **Reactivity series** — a list of metals in order of how readily they react (lose electrons).
- **Alloy** — a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements; may be substitutional or interstitial.
- **Annealing** — heating a metal and cooling it slowly to make it softer and more ductile.
- **Quenching** — heating a metal and cooling it rapidly to make it harder but more brittle.
- **Nanoparticle** — a particle between about 1 and 100 nm in size, with properties that can differ from the bulk material.

## Summary

- Metallic bonding is the attraction between a lattice of cations and a sea of delocalised electrons.
- Delocalised electrons explain electrical and thermal conductivity and lustre; non-directional bonding explains malleability and ductility.
- Stronger metallic bonding (higher cation charge, smaller cations) gives higher melting points.
- Reactivity depends on how easily a metal loses electrons; the reactivity series can be built from reactions with water, acid, oxygen and displacement.
- Alloys and heat treatment change hardness, strength and ductility by changing how easily layers slide.
- The electron-sea model cannot explain magnetism, colours or the size-dependent properties of metallic nanoparticles.

questions.prompt: According to the electron-sea model, a solid metal consists of:

options.A: a lattice of neutral atoms sharing pairs of electrons
options.B: a lattice of positive and negative ions held by electrostatic attraction
options.C: a lattice of positive ions surrounded by delocalised electrons
options.D: separate molecules held together by weak forces

questions.explanation: Metal atoms give up their valence electrons, leaving cations in a lattice surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons. Option B describes an ionic lattice, a frequent confusion because both involve cations and electrostatic attraction. Option A describes covalent bonding.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an interstitial alloy?
questions.explanation: In steel, small carbon atoms fit into the gaps between the larger iron cations, which makes it an interstitial alloy. Brass and bronze are substitutional alloys, where atoms of similar size replace some atoms of the main metal. Pure copper is not an alloy.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains why metals are malleable?

options.A: Layers of cations can slide past each other while the non-directional attraction to the delocalised electrons is maintained.
options.B: Metallic bonds are weak, so they break easily when hammered.
options.C: The delocalised electrons can absorb the energy of the hammer blow.
options.D: The metal cations repel each other, pushing the layers apart.

questions.explanation: When a force is applied, layers of cations shift, but the electron sea moves with them and the bonding is non-directional, so the structure stays held together. Option B is tempting but wrong: metallic bonding is generally strong (hence high melting points), and malleability is about bonding being kept, not broken.

questions.prompt: Why is an alloy such as steel usually harder than the pure metal it is made from?

options.A: The alloy has more delocalised electrons per atom.
options.B: The added atoms form covalent bonds that lock the lattice in place.
options.C: The alloy has a higher melting point, which always makes a material harder.
options.D: The different-sized atoms disrupt the regular layers, making it harder for layers to slide.

questions.explanation: Atoms of a different size distort the lattice, so the layers can no longer slide easily past each other, and the metal resists changing shape. Option B sounds plausible but the model explains hardness by disrupted layers, not by locking covalent bonds. Melting point and hardness (C) are not directly linked in this way.

questions.prompt: A blacksmith heats a steel blade until it glows and then plunges it into cold water. Compared with before, the blade is now:

options.A: softer and more ductile, with larger crystals
options.B: harder and more brittle, with smaller crystals
options.C: softer and more brittle, with smaller crystals
options.D: unchanged, because heat treatment only affects pure metals

questions.explanation: Rapid cooling (quenching) produces small crystals, giving a harder but more brittle metal. Option A describes annealing, which uses slow cooling. Steel is routinely heat-treated, so D is wrong.

questions.prompt: Metal W is placed in solutions containing ions of metals X, Y and Z. A coating forms when W is placed in the solutions of X and Z, but not in the solution of Y. Which conclusion is correct?

options.A: W is the most reactive of the four metals.
options.B: Y is less reactive than W.
options.C: W is more reactive than X and Z but less reactive than Y.
options.D: X is more reactive than W.

questions.explanation: A metal displaces a less reactive metal from its ions. W displaces X and Z, so it is more reactive than them; W cannot displace Y, so Y is more reactive than W. Option A ignores the 'no reaction' result with Y, which shows Y is more reactive than W.

questions.prompt: Which equation correctly represents the reaction that occurs when a strip of magnesium is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution?

options.D: No reaction occurs, because copper is more reactive than magnesium.

questions.explanation: Magnesium is above copper in the reactivity series, so it displaces copper metal from solution, forming magnesium sulfate. Option A is the reverse reaction, which does not occur because copper is less reactive. Option C is not balanced for charge (no charge on the left, 2+ on the right) and wrongly shows copper staying dissolved instead of forming a solid coating.

questions.prompt: Gold nanoparticles in solution can appear red, and they can catalyse reactions, unlike bulk gold. The best explanation is that:

options.A: the nanoparticles are made of a different isotope of gold
options.B: gold atoms change their electron configuration when divided into small pieces
options.C: nanoparticles have a very high surface area to volume ratio, so a large proportion of atoms are at the surface
options.D: the electron-sea model predicts that smaller pieces of metal are always more reactive

questions.explanation: At the nanoscale, a large fraction of the atoms are at the surface, which changes how the particles interact with light and other substances. Option D is tempting, but the electron-sea model assumes an extended lattice and cannot predict these size-dependent properties; that is one of its limitations. Isotopes (A) do not affect chemical behaviour.
